title: Electrics and starting
summary: Batteries, charging, the starter motor, glow plugs and warning lights, and the simple checks that solve most electrical starting problems.

lessons.title: Batteries
lessons.intro: A diesel engine needs no electricity to keep running, but it almost always needs a healthy battery to start. Most boats have at least two batteries, so that using the lights and instruments cannot leave you unable to start the engine.
lessons.caution: Lead-acid batteries can give off explosive hydrogen gas when charging, and they contain corrosive acid. Lithium batteries have different hazards and are managed by their own battery management system: follow their maker's instructions. With any battery, a spanner across the terminals can cause sparks, severe burns or an explosion, so keep flames and sparks away, remove metal watches and rings, and protect your eyes.

steps.title: Engine and domestic batteries
steps.text: The engine (or starting) battery is kept for starting. The domestic (or service) battery bank runs lights, instruments and other equipment. Keeping them separate means a flat domestic bank does not stop you starting the engine.

steps.title: The battery isolator
steps.text: Isolator switches disconnect the batteries from the boat's wiring. They protect against fire from faulty wiring when the boat is left, and let you choose which battery is used. Know which switch does what on your boat.

steps.title: Checking the state of charge
steps.text: A voltmeter reading taken when the battery has rested for a while, with no charging or heavy load, gives a rough guide to its state of charge. The battery maker's information explains what the readings mean for your type of battery.

steps.title: Terminals and cables
steps.text: Terminals must be clean and tight. Corrosion or a loose clamp can stop the engine starting even when the battery itself is fully charged.

steps.title: Keep them secure
steps.text: Batteries are heavy. They must be strapped down so they cannot move in rough weather, and their terminals covered so nothing can fall across them.

lessons.reviewNote: Audit note 18, revise: the hydrogen and acid warning now applies to lead-acid batteries, with a separate statement that lithium batteries have different hazards and their own management system. Please approve.

lessons.title: The alternator and charging
lessons.intro: While the engine runs, the alternator recharges the batteries and powers the boat's equipment. It is driven by a belt from the engine and controlled by a regulator that stops the batteries being overcharged.

steps.title: How it is driven
steps.text: A belt from a pulley on the crankshaft turns the alternator. If the belt is slack it slips, often squealing, and charging falls off; if it breaks, charging stops altogether.

steps.title: The regulator
steps.text: The regulator, usually built into the alternator, controls the charging voltage so the batteries are charged fully without being damaged by overcharging.

steps.title: Charging more than one battery
steps.text: Boats with separate engine and domestic batteries use a device such as a split-charge relay or a charge distributor so that both are charged while keeping them separate when the engine is stopped.

steps.title: The charge warning light
steps.text: The charge light comes on with the key before starting and should go out once the engine is running. If it stays on, or comes on while running, it indicates a charging-system fault or a failure to excite the alternator. Check the belt first, then verify using the handbook and suitable voltage checks.

steps.title: Do not break the circuit while running
steps.text: Never switch the battery isolator off while the engine is running unless the installation is specifically designed and approved for it. Suddenly disconnecting the battery can damage the alternator's electronics.

lessons.reviewNote: S09 and audit note 20, accept with qualification: a lit charge lamp now 'indicates a charging-system fault or failure to excite' rather than proving the alternator is not charging; the isolator step says 'specifically designed and approved'. Please approve.

lessons.title: The starter motor and starting circuit
lessons.intro: The starter motor has to turn a cold engine fast enough to create the compression heat that lights the fuel. It draws a very large current, which is why it has its own heavy cables and switching.

diagram.caption: A typical starting circuit. The key switch only carries a small current; the solenoid switches the heavy one.

labels.title: Battery and isolator
labels.detail: Supply the large current the starter needs.

labels.title: Key or start button
labels.detail: Sends a small current to the starter solenoid.

labels.title: Starter solenoid
labels.detail: A heavy-duty switch that connects the battery to the starter, and pushes the starter gear into mesh.

labels.title: Starter motor
labels.detail: Turns the flywheel through its toothed ring.

labels.title: Engine earth return
labels.detail: The current returns to the battery through the engine and its earth cable.

diagram.description: A flow diagram of the starting circuit in five stages: the battery and isolator, the key or start button, the starter solenoid, the starter motor turning the flywheel, and the earth return to the battery.

steps.title: The solenoid
steps.text: Turning the key sends a small current to the solenoid mounted on the starter. The solenoid pushes the starter's small gear into mesh with the flywheel and closes heavy contacts that send the battery's full current to the motor.

steps.title: The earth return
steps.text: The current has to get back to the battery. On many engines it returns through the engine block and an earth cable. A corroded or loose earth connection is an easily missed cause of starting trouble.

steps.title: Reading the symptoms
steps.text: Nothing at all usually points to the isolator, the key switch or a safety switch. A single click often means a weak battery or a poor connection. Slow turning suggests a weak battery, poor connections or a very cold engine. Normal turning without firing usually points away from the starting circuit: check the stop control, the fuel and pre-heating next (lesson 8.2).

steps.title: Safety switches
steps.text: Some installations will not let the starter turn unless the gear lever is in neutral. If nothing happens, check the lever is fully in neutral.

steps.title: Look after the starter
steps.text: Crank in short bursts with pauses between, as your handbook advises. Long cranking overheats the starter and flattens the battery, and on a wet exhaust it can let water build up: see the wet-exhaust warning at the top of this lesson.

lessons.reviewNote: S01: the wet-exhaust waterlock warning A is now shown before the steps, verbatim, because the lesson discusses cranking. Please approve.

lessons.title: Glow plugs and cold starting
lessons.intro: A cold engine soaks up the heat of compression, so on a cold day the air may not get hot enough to light the fuel. Many small diesels have a cold-starting aid, usually glow plugs, to help.

steps.title: What glow plugs do
steps.text: A glow plug is a small electric heater that pokes into each combustion chamber. Switched on before starting, it warms the air in the chamber so the fuel lights more easily.

steps.title: Pre-heating
steps.text: On many engines you hold the key in a heat position, or press a separate button, for a time before cranking. Your handbook gives the recommended time; colder weather usually needs longer.

steps.title: Other cold-start aids
steps.text: Some engines use an air intake heater instead of glow plugs, and some start well enough without any aid. A few have a cold-start device on the injection pump that adds extra fuel.

steps.title: When glow plugs fail
steps.text: A failed glow plug can show as hard starting from cold, rough running and white smoke for the first minute or so, which then clears as the engine warms. The engine often starts normally once it is warm. Other faults can cause similar symptoms, so treat these as clues rather than proof.

steps.title: Starting sprays
steps.text: Do not use aerosol starting sprays unless your engine's handbook allows them. On engines with glow plugs or intake heaters, the vapour can ignite early and cause serious engine damage.

lessons.reviewNote: Audit note 21, accept with qualification: the glow plug symptoms are now described as clues, not exclusive to glow plugs; the starting spray warning is unchanged. Please approve.

lessons.title: Warning lights and basic electrical checks
lessons.intro: The engine panel is how the engine tells you something is wrong. Knowing what each light and alarm means, and a few simple electrical checks, will solve many problems without a specialist.
lessons.caution: Remove metal watches and rings before working near batteries or the starter circuit. A short circuit can heat metal enough to cause severe burns.

steps.title: The usual lights
steps.text: Most panels have an oil pressure light, a charge light and a high temperature light, often with a buzzer. Some also have a glow plug light and gauges for temperature, oil pressure or battery voltage. Learn which is which on your own panel.

steps.title: The key-on test
steps.text: When you switch on before starting, the oil and charge lights normally come on and the alarm sounds. This shows they are working. Both lights should go out within a few seconds of the engine starting.

steps.title: Make it safe first
steps.text: Before working on any wiring, switch off the battery isolator, following your boat's own isolation procedure. On a conventional negative-earth system with lead-acid batteries, if you need to disconnect a battery, take off the negative lead first and put it back last, so a spanner touching the engine cannot cause a short circuit. Starter and house banks may be wired differently, and lithium systems often have a battery management system with their own isolation steps, so follow the installer's or maker's instructions.

steps.title: Check the connections
steps.text: Look for loose, corroded or damaged connections at the battery terminals, the isolator, the starter, the alternator and the engine earth. Green or white powder on a terminal is a sign of corrosion.

steps.title: Fuses and breakers
steps.text: The engine panel and its instruments are usually protected by a fuse or circuit breaker. If the whole panel is dead, check this before anything else.

steps.title: Use a meter
steps.text: A simple multimeter lets you compare battery voltage with the engine stopped and running, and check that power reaches each part of the circuit. Use the voltage setting across the battery terminals; never connect a meter set to measure current (amps) across a battery, which makes a short circuit and can cause burns. It is worth carrying a meter and learning the basics.

lessons.reviewNote: S10: the negative-lead-first advice is now limited to conventional negative-earth lead-acid systems, with the vessel's isolation procedure, separate starter and house banks and lithium systems covered. The meter step adds safe voltage use and a prohibition on measuring current across a battery (module 5 judgement). Please approve.

questions.prompt: Why do many boats keep a separate battery just for starting the engine?
options: So that using lights and equipment cannot leave you unable to start
Because the engine needs two batteries to turn over
Because domestic batteries cannot be charged by the engine's alternator
So the engine can run without an alternator
questions.explanation: If the domestic bank is run flat overnight, the separate engine battery still has the charge needed to start, and the engine can then recharge both.

questions.prompt: The battery is fully charged but the starter only clicks. What should you check first?
options: That the battery terminals are clean and tight
That the engine oil level is not too high
That the raw water strainer basket is clear of weed
That nothing is caught round the propeller
questions.explanation: A loose or corroded terminal cannot pass the heavy starting current, even from a good battery, so it behaves like a flat one.

questions.prompt: Why is a voltmeter reading of a battery's state of charge best taken after it has rested?
options: Recent charging or heavy use shifts the voltage, giving a misleading reading
The meter needs time to charge itself up from the battery first
A battery gives no voltage reading at all while it is in use
Resting lets any gas escape so the meter can make contact
questions.explanation: Just after charging the voltage is higher than the true state of charge, and under load it is lower. After a rest it settles to a value that better reflects the charge.

questions.prompt: Why should sparks and flames be kept away from lead-acid batteries that are being charged?
options: Charging can give off hydrogen gas, which is explosive
Sparks can damage the charger's electronics
Heat from a flame makes the battery overcharge
A spark can reverse the battery's polarity
questions.explanation: Vented lead-acid batteries can release hydrogen while charging. In a poorly ventilated locker, a spark from a loose connection or a dropped tool can ignite it. Lithium batteries do not give off hydrogen in normal use but have hazards of their own.
questions.reviewNote: Audit note 19, revise: the question is now limited to lead-acid batteries, and the explanation says lithium hazards differ. Please approve.

questions.prompt: What drives the alternator?
options: A belt from the engine's crankshaft pulley
The battery
The propeller shaft, through the gearbox
An electric motor powered from the domestic bank
questions.explanation: The alternator is turned by a belt from the engine, so it only charges while the engine runs and the belt is in good order.

questions.prompt: The charge warning light stays on after the engine has started. What does this indicate?
options: A charging-system fault, or the alternator failing to excite
The batteries are fully charged and now resting
The alternator has definitely failed and needs replacing
The engine coolant is starting to overheat
questions.explanation: The light points to a fault somewhere in the charging system, not necessarily the alternator itself. Check the belt and connections, then verify with the handbook and a voltage check; see Not charging in the Fault finder.
questions.reviewNote: S09: the key no longer says the lamp proves the alternator is not charging. Please approve.

questions.prompt: What is the regulator's job?
options: Controlling the charging voltage to avoid overcharging
Keeping the engine speed steady as the load changes
Switching the starter motor on when you turn the key to start
Measuring the oil pressure and lighting the warning
questions.explanation: Without regulation the alternator's output would rise with engine speed and could damage the batteries. The regulator holds the voltage at a safe charging level.

questions.prompt: Why should you not normally switch off the battery isolator while the engine is running?
options: Cutting off the battery can damage the alternator's electronics
The engine will stop at once without battery power
It drains the batteries back through the alternator instead
The starter motor can engage while the engine is running
questions.explanation: With the battery disconnected, the alternator's output has nowhere to go and the voltage can spike, damaging its diodes or regulator. A diesel keeps running without the battery.

questions.prompt: What does the starter motor turn to start the engine?
options: The flywheel, through its toothed ring
The camshaft, through its drive chain
The propeller shaft, through the gearbox
The crankshaft pulley, through the belt
questions.explanation: The starter's small gear meshes with the teeth around the flywheel, which is bolted to the crankshaft, and turns the engine over.

questions.prompt: Why is a solenoid used in the starting circuit?
options: So the key's small current can switch the starter's large one
To store a charge of electricity, ready for the next start
To heat the air in the cylinders before starting
To charge the battery while the engine is cranking
questions.explanation: The starter draws far more current than a key switch could handle. The solenoid is a heavy-duty switch that the key operates with a small current.

questions.prompt: When you press the start button, nothing happens at all, not even a click. Which of these is a likely cause?
options: The battery isolator is off or the gear lever is not in neutral
Air has been drawn into the fuel system through a loose joint
The raw water strainer is blocked with weed and debris
The engine oil level is below the minimum mark
questions.explanation: Complete silence usually means no current is reaching the solenoid. Fuel, cooling and oil problems do not stop the starter turning.

questions.prompt: The battery is good and its terminals are clean, but the starter turns slowly. Which connection is often overlooked?
options: The engine earth cable
The glow plug feed wire
The alternator output terminal
The fuse for the engine panel
questions.explanation: Starting current returns to the battery through the engine and its earth cable. Corrosion there adds resistance and slows the starter just like a weak battery. The glow plug and alternator wiring do not carry starting current, and a blown panel fuse would stop the starter altogether.

questions.prompt: What does a glow plug do?
options: Heats the combustion chamber to help a cold engine start
Creates a spark to light the fuel while the engine is running
Warms the fuel in the filter so it flows in cold weather
Warms the engine oil in the sump
questions.explanation: A diesel has no spark. The glow plug is a small heater used before and during starting so the compressed air gets hot enough to light the fuel.

questions.prompt: Why does a diesel engine find it harder to start on a cold day?
options: Cold metal soaks up the compression heat, so the air may not get hot enough
Cold air holds too little oxygen for the fuel to burn
The starter motor is designed to work only in warm weather
Diesel stops flowing as soon as it drops below room temperature
questions.explanation: Compression ignition depends on the air getting very hot. A cold block and head draw heat out of the air, which is why pre-heating helps.

questions.prompt: An engine is hard to start from cold and smokes white for a minute, then runs well and restarts easily when warm. What is a likely cause?
options: A failed glow plug or a fault in the glow plug circuit
A raw water strainer partly blocked with weed
An alternator belt that is slipping on its drive pulley
Too much oil in the sump after an oil change
questions.explanation: These are classic signs of poor cold starting. Once warm, the engine does not need the glow plugs, so it runs and restarts normally.

questions.prompt: Why can aerosol starting sprays be dangerous in an engine with glow plugs?
options: The vapour can ignite early on the hot plugs and damage the engine
The spray gets into the fuel and blocks the fine filter
The spray stops the alternator charging the battery
The spray chills the glow plugs so they stop heating
questions.explanation: Starting spray is highly flammable. Lit by a hot glow plug or intake heater before the piston is in position, it can cause violent combustion that damages the engine. Only use it if the handbook allows.

questions.prompt: When you switch on before starting, which lights would you normally expect to come on?
options: The oil pressure and charge warning lights
None at all
The oil pressure light alone; the charge light comes on once the engine runs
The high temperature light, which stays on while running
questions.explanation: With the engine stopped there is no oil pressure and no charging, so both lights come on. That shows they work. They should go out soon after starting.

questions.prompt: On a conventional negative-earth system with lead-acid batteries, which lead should you take off first when disconnecting a battery?
options: The negative lead
The positive lead
Either, it makes no difference
Whichever is easier to reach
questions.explanation: On these systems the engine is connected to the negative side. With the negative removed first, a spanner touching the positive terminal and the engine cannot complete a circuit and cause a short. Other systems, such as lithium banks with a battery management system, may have their own isolation procedure.

questions.prompt: The whole engine panel is dead when you turn the key. What should you check early on?
options: The battery isolator and the panel's fuse or circuit breaker
The engine oil level, in case the panel has shut off
The fuel filter, in case it is blocked with sludge
The raw water impeller, in case its vanes have broken off
questions.explanation: If nothing at all lights, power is not reaching the panel. The isolator, fuse or breaker are the simplest things that cut it off.

questions.prompt: Why should you remove metal rings and watches before working near the batteries?
options: A short circuit through the metal can heat it and cause severe burns
Metal jewellery near the terminals slowly drains the battery's charge
They interfere with the multimeter's voltage readings
They attract corrosion onto the battery terminals
questions.explanation: A battery can deliver a very large current. If a ring bridges a live terminal and earth, it heats almost instantly and can burn deeply.

questions.prompt: You want to check a battery with a multimeter. Which setting and connection is safe?
options: The voltage setting, with the probes across the battery terminals
The current (amps) setting, with the probes across the battery terminals
The resistance setting, with the engine running
The current setting, with one probe on the engine and one on the positive terminal
questions.explanation: A meter on its voltage setting has a high resistance, so it can be connected across the battery safely. On a current setting it is close to a short circuit: connected across a battery or to earth it can blow the meter, burn the leads and burn you.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.1 (module 5 judgement, S20): safe multimeter use. Please approve.
